paper_title: Glyph: An Interpretability Engine for AI-Driven Scientific Discovery in Clinical Data

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Automated scientific discovery has the potential to advance understanding of disease mechanisms and accelerate identification of early disease markers. Manual data annotation is infeasible at population scale, motivating methods that automatically extract pre-defined phenotypes in multimodal and unstructured clinical data. Such pre-defined feature sets determine and limit which associations these approaches can discover. This limitation extends to agentic AI systems that use these tools to query population-scale data. In contrast, foundation models (FMs) trained on large volumes of clinical data can perform tasks beyond their training objectives. This suggests their latent embeddings may represent novel or unexplored features that could yield insights into disease mechanisms, yet such latent features remain difficult to interpret. To address this challenge, we introduce Glyph, an automated multistage framework that extracts features from multimodal and unstructured clinical data using FMs and sparse autoencoders, interprets them as coded clinical concepts, and evaluates their value for clinical scientific discovery. We applied Glyph to abdominal CT volumes, CT radiology reports and laboratory measurements from 41,628 patients across different institutions. We identified 397 predictive concepts supported by 4,463 Bonferroni-significant associations. Moreover, a majority of discovered associations were automatically reproducible in held-out cohorts across different sites. Glyph concepts provided complementary associations to literature-derived markers, leading to gains in predictive power. We envision that interpretability can extend beyond a mechanistic understanding of neural networks to connecting implicitly learned features with clinical knowledge and establishing their significance for patient outcomes. We release Glyph at https://github.com/StanfordMIMI/Glyph.

sections.title: ABSTRACT
sections.content: Automated scientific discovery has the potential to advance understanding of disease mechanisms and accelerate identification of early disease markers1. Manual data annotation is infeasible at population scale, motivating methods that automatically extract pre-defined phenotypes in multimodal and unstructured clinical data2, 3. Such pre-defined feature sets determine and limit which associations these approaches can discover. This limitation extends to agentic AI systems that use these tools to query population-scale data4, 5. In contrast, foundation models (FMs) trained on large volumes of clinical data can perform tasks beyond their training objectives6. This suggests their latent embeddings may represent novel or unexplored features that could yield insights into disease mechanisms, yet such latent features remain diﬀicult to interpret. To address this challenge, we introduce Glyph, an automated multistage framework that extracts features from multimodal and unstructured clinical data using FMs and sparse autoencoders, interprets them as coded clinical concepts, and evaluates their value for clinical scientific discovery. We applied Glyph to multimodal clinical data consisting of abdominal CT volumes, CT radiology reports and laboratory measurements from 41,628 patients across different institutions. At the discovery site, we tested 604,185 conceptoutcome associations, focusing on 141 prognostic outcomes most strongly predicted by FM embeddings. This yielded 397 predictive concepts supported by 4,463 Bonferroni-significant associations, recovering established prognostic relationships across several disease axes, including hepatic, renal, cardiovascular and oncologic disease. Moreover, majority of discovered associations were automatically reproducible in held-out cohorts across different sites. Separating embeddings into concepts further enabled confounder adjustment that attenuated associations with markers of general illness severity, preserved key disease-specific associations and revealed independent systemic risk markers. Compared with disease markers obtained from automated literature search, disease associations of the top ten Glyph concepts were reproduced more frequently in the pooled held-out cohort with significantly larger median odds ratios. This revealed gaps in the clinical literature, highlighting the underexplored prognostic value of Glyph concepts, suggesting new predictive targets. We envision that interpretability can extend beyond mechanistic understanding of neural networks to connecting implicitly learned features with clinical knowledge and establishing their significance for patient outcomes. We release Glyph at https://github.com/StanfordMIMI/Glyph to enable and share discoveries in other clinical domains. Correspondence: robbie.holland@stanford.edu Co-senior authors.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Identifying early disease markers has repeatedly transformed clinical practice and patient outcomes7. Clinical discovery is inherently challenging as evidence of potentially novel markers is captured across diverse, often unstructured and high-dimensional modalities, including 2D and 3D imaging, laboratory results, and textual reports6. Moreover, the growing volume of clinical data, including approximately 300 million CT scans acquired worldwide each year8, creates opportunities to identify new markers and uncover unknown associations with broader range of clinical outcomes. Yet this growth also highlights gap in our ability to process these data at scale, given the time and expertise required to manually define, annotate, and validate candidate disease markers. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly proposed as means of accelerating scientific discovery1. In protein folding and materials science, targeted models have sharply reduced the time and cost of identifying promising candidates911. Attempts to automate clinical science have searched large databases of manually coded phenotypes through phenome-wide association studies (PheWAS)2, 12. Efforts to accelerate this approach use deep learning or agents to automate the annotation of phenotypes directly from images, but still restricts investigation to preselected set of chosen markers3, 4, 13. As result, clinical discovery still lacks an eﬀicient framework for identifying open-ended, reproducible, and independent disease markers within multimodal data. One potential solution lies in foundation model (FM) embeddings. Trained on large volumes of multimodal medical data, FMs produce embeddings that characterize patient states14. Such embeddings have been observed to perform well on tasks they were not explicitly trained for1417, including disease prognosis and risk stratification, suggesting that they contain clinically meaningful associations beyond their original training objectives. However, these markers remain entangled within high-dimensional vectors, making them diﬀicult to isolate and evaluate as candidate markers. Recently, mechanistic interpretability1820 has emerged as self-supervised approach to uncover interpretable concepts encoded within FM embeddings, without the need for prospective annotation. Yet its broader potential for transforming FMs into engines of clinical discovery remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we introduce Glyph, framework that turns foundation model (FM) embeddings into concepts for clinical discovery. The name derives from glyph, or symbol that conveys meaning, reflecting our goal of giving hidden information form that can be studied. Drawing on mechanistic interpretability, Glyph discovers coded concepts directly in FM embeddings and detects them across patients without requiring candidate markers to be defined and annotated in advance. These extracted concepts are measurable, interpretable patterns in patient data that together preserve the FMs predictive capacity. Glyph integrates them with established clinical variables and tests their associations with disease-related outcomes across patient populations. This enables eﬀicient, closedand open-ended discovery that is infeasible with embeddings alone or with agentic systems operating on limited set of pre-defined concepts. Our contributions are as follows: 1. Establishing the concept space. To make FM embeddings useful for discovery, we develop the Glyph framework to first represent such embeddings in sets of sparse features, and then filter and interpret these as clinically meaningful concepts. Specifically, we evaluated features for significant prognostic associations, reproducibility across three sites, persistence after adjustment for measured confounders, and overall interpretability. Glyph identified 397 predictive concepts bearing 4,463 significant associations to 141 future disease outcomes meeting Bonferroni threshold of 8.28 108. Identifying concepts with at least one significant association yielded space of high-risk concepts, capturing disease risk across modalities. Concept interpretations and prognostic associations also reproduced in external cohorts. 2. Rediscovery and discovery. The validated concept space recovered established prognostic relationships across several disease axes, including hepatic, renal, cardiovascular, and oncologic disease. When tested in held-out cohorts, these associations reproduced across institutions. Glyph then extended these findings by linking established risk markers to additional outcomes and identifying reproducible prognostic associations that remain poorly characterized in the literature. Beyond disease-specific risk profiles, Glyph identified systemic risk markers across modalities, with one 2/36 Figure 1. Transforming foundation model embeddings into engines of clinical discovery. Glyph can be applied to any data expected to contain useful markers for discovery. Foundation models compress multimodal clinical data into high-dimensional embeddings, typically used for predefined prediction tasks. The structural contents of embeddings driving these predictions is typically not unexplored. Glyph instead transforms FM embeddings into engines for discovery, mapping space of concepts hidden within these embeddings. Glyph goes beyond embeddings by decomposing them into sparse concepts that can be studied individually and in selected combinations (Figure 1c). Glyph concepts recover associations established in clinical research and ICD-based PheWAS analyses, while revealing complementary associations not yet discovered by either approach. ef Glyph evaluates concepts for associations with future disease after correction for multiple testing, associations that persist after adjustment for measured confounders, and clinical interpretability. All findings are tested for reproducibility across multiple cohorts. Validated concepts provide an interface for asking complex questions of FM embeddings and grounding the answers in the underlying data. 3/36 imaging and three laboratory concepts retaining broad associations across disease groups after adjustment for potential confounders. Glyph revealed that nearly half of the high-risk imaging concepts were not consistently documented in the accompanying radiology reports. 3. Comparison with literature We investigated whether and in which domains Glyph brought additional prognostic value over the clinical literature. To this end, co-scientist agent processed 342,647 clinical papers covering each discovery axes, and reproduced 412 published markers in our data. We found using just ten Glyph concepts per axis led to significantly stronger models in external data than literature markers alone (3.34% AUC gain, = 2.66 1028), with predictive improvements of up to 11.7% in specific axes. Comparing the top ten Glyph concepts with the top ten literature markers per outcome, selected at the Discovery Site, Glyph associations reproduced more frequently in the pooled held-out cohort (64.8% vs. 41.2%, = 2.54 106) at higher median confounder-adjusted odds ratios (1.31 vs. 1.16, = 5.0 105). 4. Comparison with pre-coded phenotypes Similarly, we also asked whether pre-coded phenotypes could support the same discoveries, comparing Glyph with an automated PheWAS-style analysis of ICD-derived Phecodes. Across the same outcomes, associations from Glyph reproduced more often than those from Phecodes at Internal Test (69.3% vs. 49.1%, = 9.77 104) and External Site #1 (74.3% vs. 63.9%, = 2.93 103), and had larger median effect sizes. Overall, Glyph showed complementary benefit to existing disease coding protocols and clinical literature. 5. Open-source and use. Glyph extracts additional value from existing pretrained FMs, without retraining. To enable researchers to find our concept space in their cohorts, or build new concept spaces from their data, we open-source Glyph at github.com/StanfordMIMI/Glyph, installable via pip install glyph-discovery. validated concept space also supports other applications including explainable patient-level predictions and retrieval. We also release the Glyph MCP, enabling clinicians, engineers, and AI agents to investigate patient data and test open-ended hypotheses and applications through concepts.

sections.title: 2 Results
sections.content: Glyph was deployed in multimodal Discovery Site cohort of 14,652 patients, comprising 20,391 3D abdominal CT volumes (3,262,560 preprocessed slices), radiology reports (8,083,882 tokens), and 1,588,003 lab entries spanning 350 types (Figure 1a). These three modalities were embedded using the Merlin image encoder14, Qwen3-Embedding-8B21, and Labs FM, respectively (Figure 1b). Glyph then decomposes these embeddings into sets of sparse features (Figure 1c). We identified when Glyph concepts rediscovered established prognostic associations, and when they reveal complementary associations absent from the literature or not discoverable by automated PheWAS-style discovery analysis (Figure 1d). To enable this analysis, we developed rigorous pipeline to process sparse features in embeddings as concepts useful for discovery (Figure 1eg). To maximize discovery yield, we used the Discovery Site validation set to identify 141 disease outcomes whose onset 14 years after abdominal CT was most predictable from FM embeddings (see Methods, Section 4.5). These outcomes spanned hepatic, renal, cardiovascular, metabolic, and neurological disease. To surface high-risk concepts, Glyph filters features to those with at least one significant prognostic association (Figure 1e), before assessing their independent risk adjusted for specific confounders (Figure 1f), and estimating each featuress clinical interpretation (Figure 1g). At each step, we assessed the reproducibility of these analyses across three held-out cohorts comprising 26,976 patients and 45,139 CT studies, with 7,222,240 preprocessed CT slices, 14,342,345 radiology-report tokens, and 2,184,424 lab entries (Figure 1h). This pipeline led to the set of 397 highrisk concepts that can be used in downstream discovery workflows (Figure 1i).

sections.title: 2.1 Glyph discovered a clinical concept space in FM embeddings
sections.content: To first identify pool of candidate features, Glyph fits one SAE architecture per modality (Figure 2a). On the Discovery Site, SAEs identified 3,315 features in embeddings of reports, 343 in images, and 627 in labs, totaling 4,285 features. Once features are learned, they can be re-extracted elsewhere without 4/36 Figure 2. The Glyph framework. An interactive version is available at https://stanfordmimi.github.io/Glyph-research/. At the Discovery Site, Glyph trains sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to decompose foundation model (FM) embeddings into sparse concepts. Each SAE encoder is then frozen as concept extractor and its decoder discarded. Concepts are re-extracted zero-shot in held-out internal and external cohorts to assess reproducibility of their interpretations, prognostic associations, and confounder analyses. The discovered concept space maps the clinical characteristics and disease burden of patients undergoing abdominal CT at the Discovery Site, alongside routine variables such as age and smoking status. We show 397 concepts (9.26% of the 4,285 candidate features) that were associated with at least one of the 141 prognostic outcomes after Bonferroni correction. Edges show correlations between concepts in the top 2.5%. Clinically related concepts were found to cluster into subregions (dashed boxes) corresponding to liver, renal, and cardiovascular disease, and systemic inflammatory and cholestatic illness. Node size scales with the logarithm of the number of patients who share the specific concept. confounder-adjusted version of this network is shown in Figure 11. 5/36 recalibration (Figure 2b). Specifically, FMs were reapplied to extract embeddings of data in the Internal Test, External Site #1 and External Site #2 cohorts. The trained SAEs were then applied zero-shot to each sites embeddings to re-extract the same set of 4,285 features. Overall, these features preserved the majority of the original embeddings variance and predictive performance (see Extended Figure 7 and Section 4.3). These features were then filtered by Glyphs discovery pipeline, explored in detail in Sections 2.2, 2.3 and Section A.1, yielding the set of 397 validated, high-risk concepts. Textual interpretations of these concepts were then attempted via contrastive approach detailed in Section A.1 and illustrated in Figure 12. Throughout, we refer to concepts by modality-prefixed index: for radiology report, for imaging, and for laboratory concepts. High-risk concepts clustered into neighborhoods reflecting liver, kidney, cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, and malignant disease, as well as inflammatory states and abnormal cholesterol (Figure 2c). Within the liver and kidney neighborhoods, granular concepts from different modalities overlapped. Concepts for fluid accumulation, including effusions and ascites, lay nearby and were closely correlated with laboratory concepts reflecting hypoalbuminemia, reflecting known comorbidities to liver cirrhosis22. Laboratory concepts also provided information complementary to imaging and reports, such as evidence of abnormal cholesterol, situated adjacent to kidney disease23, and inflammatory markers. Other regions contained high-risk imaging concepts with no corresponding report concepts, suggesting radiological features that are not routinely documented. The concept space also isolated the presence of medical devices, including tubes and drains, and postsurgical artifacts, that could confound predictions based on whole embeddings. It also integrated established variables not derived from SAEs, such as patient age and smoking status, alongside the extracted concepts, situating these adjacent to cardiovascular and musculoskeletal disease, which are also known correlates24. These 397 high-risk concepts are explored for their discovery potential in the remainder of the paper.

sections.title: 2.2 Glyph identified reproducible markers of future disease risk
sections.content: Having constructed the concept space, we tested whether it contained any significant, reproducible highrisk markers for future disease onset. Because the cohort consisted of patients who underwent abdominal ICD codes provided broad, CT, associations were expected to be enriched for abdominal pathology. cross-institutional outcome labels but may be affected by undercoding, miscoding, delayed entry, and institutional differences in coding practices. Associations may also reflect clinical workflows, motivating the confounder analysis in Section 2.3. To identify high-risk concepts, we first computed per-standard-deviation odds ratios (ORs) between all pairings of 4,285 features and 141 outcomes, yielding 604,185 candidate associations at the Discovery Site. These comprised 467,415 radiology report, 48,363 imaging, and 88,407 laboratory associations (Figure 3a; see Methods, Section 4.6). To set stringent threshold for evidence, we applied the Discovery filter, requiring Bonferroni-corrected 8.28 108 and OR > 1.0 (Figure 3b). This analysis uncovered 4,463 significant associations (0.739% of all pairs), establishing that the concept space contains signals of future disease across radiology reports (858; 0.184%), imaging (2,251; 4.65%), and laboratory measurements (1,354; 1.53%). This narrowed the space to the 397 high-risk concepts with at least one significant association used in the remainder of the analyses (as shown in Figure 2b). Having identified thousands of significant associations, we then assessed whether any were reproducible in the internal and external sites. This was tested using less conservative Reproducibility filter, affording 5% false discovery rate via the BenjaminiHochberg procedure (see Methods, Section 4.7). Of the 4,463 promising associations, 3,095 (69.3%) were reproduced without calibration on the Internal Test cohort of 3,667 patients (see Figure 3c). Remarkably, greater number, 3,314 (74.3%), were reproduced at the secondary site, External Site #1, reflecting its larger cohort of 17,224 patients and indicating that associations generalized across institutions. Moreover, External Site #2 which was out of state, reproduced 1,701 (54.7%) of the radiology-report and imaging associations, reinforcing the generalizability of these findings across institutions. Overall, this showed that Glyph automatically surfaced concepts that were reproducibly predictive of future disease across patient populations. This prompted us to investigate the nature of these associations, and whether they reflected insights in the literature. Discovery filter (p 0.05 adjusted for multiple testing via Bonferroni correction, equivalent to 8.28 108, and OR > 1.0) applied on the Discovery Site yields 4,463 (0.739%) promising associations. These rediscoveries recapitulated well established risk factors across hepatic, renal, and cardiovascular disease, and reveal several systemic risk factors in our data. Rediscovery of hepatic disease progression: Among the strongest predictors of hepatic disease were L108 (cholestasis), I65 (splenomegaly), I21 (ascites) and R85 (liver cirrhosis and varices). R85 predicted future primary liver cancer with odds ratios and p-values of 2.45 = 1.2 1039, 2.55 = 1.2 107, 1.73 = 1.3109, 1.64 = 5.7109 at the Discovery Site, Internal Test, External Site #1 and External Site #2, respectively (Figure 4f). It was also associated with portal hypertension (OR 2.193.57), with both associations replicating across all four cohorts. These findings accord with established complications of cirrhosis25, 26. R85 was associated with the onset of 39 of 141 outcomes (Figure 3e), tracing the recognised natural history of cirrhosis through jaundice, hepatic necrosis, varices, splenomegaly and coagulopathy. Associations also extended to renal, respiratory and infection diagnoses, consistent with reported evidence of these conditions in patients with cirrhosis2729. L108 also recovered the majority of hepatic outcomes. These included future primary liver cancer (OR 2.082.57) and portal hypertension (OR 1.632.92). Li and Apte linked bile-acid accumulation in cholestasis to liver injury and cancer30, but did not evaluate any prognostic relationships. Reproducible associations extended to future liver transplantation and coagulation (see Figure 3g). Rediscovery of renal disease progression: The strongest marker of renal disease was L84 (azotemia), which reproducibly traced the stages and complications of chronic kidney disease, including chronic renal failure (2.022.52), progression to stage IV disease (1.772.73), initiation of renal dialysis (2.043.21), eventual kidney transplantation (2.532.87), and the metabolic consequences of uremia in anaemia of chronic kidney disease (1.872.44) and hyperkalaemia (1.802.07)31. L84 also extended beyond renal disease to cardiovascular, metabolic, infectious, respiratory, hepatic and haematological outcomes. Elevated blood urea nitrogen (BUN), measure of azotemia, predicted mortality after acute coronary syndromes in prior work, although that study did not examine later diagnoses across disease groups32. By comparison, L69 (impaired renal function, defined by increased creatinine and BUN and reduced eGFR) was far more specific, as its seven significant associations were all renal (against 11 for L84 among 76 spanning every disease group). Its effects were smaller on all four shared outcomes (1.091.54 versus 1.772.87), it did not predict dialysis initiation or acute renal failure. Notably, urinary protein loss was not isolated by any single concept, despite albuminuria being second axis of chronic kidney disease staging alongside eGFR31; nephrotic-range values were distributed among concepts dominated by hypoalbuminaemia (L34, L45, L61, L87). Unlike the hepatic rediscoveries, no radiological concept captured renal disease progression, consistent with the weak association between visible kidney structure and renal function33. Specifically, R398 (kidney atrophy) and R302 (polycystic kidney disease) reached only modest effect sizes (1.161.41) and replicated inconsistently. By contrast, I109 (aortic calcification) and L127 (cytopenia) were associated with 10 and 12 of 13 renal outcomes, respectively, with strong reproduction across cohorts. Prior studies established abdominal aortic calcification as cardiovascular prognostic marker in CKD34; here it also marked later renal diagnoses more consistently than kidney-specific imaging findings. Rediscovery of cardiovascular risk markers: Glyph recovered early cardiovascular markers of calcification and atherosclerosis. Specifically, R21 (calcification of the coronary arteries or cardiac valves) was prominent report-derived cardiovascular predictor, reproducibly predicting myocardial infarction (OR 1.251.70), heart failure with preserved (1.581.83) and reduced (1.401.92) ejection fraction, and coronary atherosclerosis (1.521.97). Prospective studies have linked coronary and mitral annular calcification to subsequent cardiovascular events35, 36. Both R21 and R3 (moderate to severe atherosclerotic disease) replicated strongly at External Sites #1 and #2 (R21: 100% and 73.7%; R3: 91.7% and 86.1%), well above the 33.8% cohort average at External Site #2. Imaging concepts outperformed report-based concepts: the imaging group, comprising I109 (abdominal aortic calcification), I15 (abdominopelvic atherosclerosis) and I26 (aortic atherosclerosis; Figure 3e), covered 23 of 28 cardiovascular outcomes (82.1%), against 19 of 28 (67.9%) for the report-based group, and replicated more consistently across the Internal Test and External Sites #1 and #2 (96.1%, 98.7% and 8/36 93.4% versus 89.6%, 97.9% and 70.8%). Imaging concepts also more strongly recovered atherosclerosiss known systemic vascular effects, covering more outcomes and with larger effect sizes than report-based concepts across renal (11 of 13, 84.6% vs. 7 of 13, 53.8%) and neurocognitive outcomes (8 of 12, 66.7% vs. 6 of 12, 50.0%)37, including vascular dementia38. Atherosclerosis and vascular calcification concepts (I26, I106, R21 and R420) also showed associations beyond cardiovascular disease, including with femoral and vertebral fractures39 and chondrocalcinosis. Most inflammatory concepts (L0, L3, L4, L8, L92) did not have substantial associations with cardiovascular outcomes, which was unexpected given the established role of inflammation in atherosclerosis40. L68, more indicative of infection (a blood-count pattern with elevated neutrophils, white cells, monocytes and platelets) than auto-immune inflammation, was associated with 5 of the 28 cardiovascular outcomes. It reproducibly predicted ischaemic heart disease (OR 1.171.33) and myocardial infarction (1.211.34). L121 captured delayed cardiac conduction on ECG and was associated with later arrhythmia and heart failure, consistent with prospective evidence linking prolonged QRS duration to incident heart failure41. L1488 similarly captured abnormal RR intervals, but neither concepts adjusted associations reproduced consistently, and both may reflect ECG testing prompted by suspected cardiac disease. Concepts capturing abnormal cholesterol (L182, L184, L481, L852) did not emerge as major cardiovascular risk markers in this cohort, despite the established causal role of LDL cholesterol in atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease42, potentially due to widespread use of statins in this cohort. Concepts encoding systemic risk markers: Beyond organ-specific associations, several concepts behaved as broad markers of systemic risk, each associated with more than half of the outcomes tested and spanning nearly every disease group. L127 (cytopenia) and L108 (cholestasis) had the broadest risk profiles, associated with 89 (63.1%) and 87 of 141 outcomes (61.7%) respectively, each spanning 10 of 11 disease groups. L108 extended beyond liver disease to predict future infection, electrolyte disturbance, renal failure and cardiac failure. Cholemic nephropathy offers one possible explanation for these renal associations in patients with severe liver disease43, 44. L127 (cytopenia) likewise reached cardiovascular, infectious, renal and metabolic outcomes. L84 (azotemia) followed with 76 associations (53.9%) and spanned all 11 groups. This breadth generalized across institutions: L108 reproduced 82 of its 87 associations at the Internal Test cohort (94%) and 84 (97%) at External Site #1, L127 79 (89%) and 86 (97%), and L84 69 (91%) and 75 (99%), each well above the cohort-wide rates of 69.3% and 74.3%. Fluid accumulation behaved similarly: I21 (ascites) was associated with 68 outcomes across 10 groups and carried the largest single effect of any systemic concept (OR up to 3.17), while I25 (combined ascites, anasarca and effusion) reached 62 outcomes across all 11 groups, and R101 (pleural effusion with ascites) 30. I28 (findings of chronic or end-stage disease) contributed an imaging-derived systemic marker, associated with 84 outcomes (59.6%) across 10 groups and reproducing 76 (90%) and 83 (99%) times. Notably, ascites reproduced least consistently of this set (48 of 68, 71%, and 46, 68%), an early indication that its breadth may rest on shared upstream disease rather than independent risk, which we examine in Section 2.3. second family encoded hypoalbuminaemia and anaemia (L34, L59, L77, L82, L87, L91, L124), each associated with 39 to 71 outcomes across 10 disease groups with median odds ratios of 1.42 to 1.62. Infection and sepsis: L127 (cytopenia)45 and L108 (cholestasis) were each associated with 14 of 22 subsequent infectious and inflammatory outcomes, although neither was specific to this outcome group. I76 (severely distended bowel pattern) was associated with 5 of 20, including bacterial pneumonia, sepsis and septicemia, although presence of this image phenotype was not consistently documented in the corresponding radiology reports. Visual review identified severely distended, fluid-filled bowel loops (Figure 12de; see Section A.1). This recapitulates prior evidence linking bowel obstruction to bacterial translocation and postoperative septic complications46. Rediscovery of metastatic sequelae R64 (metastatic disease) predicted systemic complications of advanced malignancy, including cachexia and pancytopenia (Discovery ORs 1.631.85, both reproducing at Internal Test and External Site #1), capturing the wasting and marrow failure of disseminated disease47, alongside neutropenia, bacteremia, and septic shock (ORs 1.451.58, same replication pattern), reflecting common infectious complications48. Overall, while 25 of R64s 32 significant associations (78%) replicated at Internal Test and 26 (81%) at External Site #1, none reproduced at External Site #2, likely 9/36 due to differences in coding practices.

sections.title: 2.3 Glyph enabled confounder analysis to identify independent disease markers
sections.content: Having identified significant, reproducible disease markers, we assessed whether they persisted after adjustment by potential confounders. concept encoding ascites may appear to predict liver cancer because underlying cirrhosis can cause both fluid accumulation and an increased risk of liver cancer (see Figure 4a). The majority of FM outputs are only tested for predictive correlation to an outcome, and rarely test if this prediction is potentially confounded. This extends the scientific reach of foundation models from correlation towards independence analysis. Glyph concepts, due to being both interpretable and sparse, can be tested for independence alongside known clinical covariates and risk markers in confounder analysis frameworks. As in the association study, these results identify associations that persist after adjustment for measured clinical variables and other concepts, rather than establish causality. We adjusted each significant association for confounders by applying double machine learning (DML) (see Figure 4b and Methods, Section 4.8). 16 confounders were drawn per-outcome, including the top 10 significantly associated concepts, and six universal clinical covariates covering age, sex, race, BMI, alcohol use, and smoking. Applying the Confounder filter to the 4,463 promising associations on the Discovery Site, 1,198 (26.8%) retained an adjusted OR > 1.0 (Figure 4c). Fewer associations were retained at the Internal Test Site and External Sites #1 and #2, potentially reflecting lower statistical power, variation in FM reproducibility, and differences in population distributions. At External Site #2, 643 of 3,109 associations (20.7%) survived the Confounder filter. In the following, we study which significant associations withstood adjustment, while also noting groups of concepts that were most heavily attenuated. Unless otherwise specified, results refer to the Discovery Site. Independence of hepatic disease risk markers: R85 (cirrhotic liver morphology and varices) was associated with 9 of 11 hepatic outcomes at the Discovery Site, and 6 of these 9 remained significant after confounder adjustment (see Figure 4d). Among these were known consequences of cirrhosis, including portal hypertension (adjusted OR 2.46 = 3.0 104, 2.35 = 1.4 101, 3.10 = 1.2 103, 1.77 = 2.3 109), liver abscesses (2.98 = 1.5 1016, 3.15 = 2.7 108, 3.19 = 1.1 107, 1.87 = 1.4 1011), primary liver cancer (4.07 = 1.2 1071, 2.13 = 4.1 107, 1.79 = 1.9 108, 1.68 = 2.4 107) and liver transplantation (2.11 = 1.6 108, 2.06 = 1.0 107, 2.15 = 1.0 1010, 0.99 = 9.8 101), with reproduction across all three held-out cohorts in the majority of cases. By contrast, I21 (ascites) and I25 (ascites, anasarca or pleural effusion) retained only one of 10 and none of eight Discovery Site associations, respectively, after adjustment that included R85. This pattern is consistent with fluid accumulation being less specific to hepatic disease than cirrhotic morphology and varices26. Independence of renal disease risk markers: As in hepatic disease, confounder adjustment concentrated the renal signal on known markers of renal disease. L84 (azotemia) retained 8 of its 11 Discovery Site renal associations, covering chronic renal failure, stage IV disease, kidney transplantation, oliguria and anuria, hypertensive chronic kidney disease, secondary hyperparathyroidism, acute renal failure and the composite chronic kidney disease outcome, with effects broadly unchanged by adjustment (ORs 1.71 2.53 vs. adjusted ORs 1.272.95). L69 (impaired renal function) retained 6 of its 7 associations, all renal, at consistently smaller effects (ORs 1.241.44 vs. adjusted ORs 1.451.85), remaining highly concentrated on the kidney. The broader I109 (aortic calcification) and L127 (cytopenia) markers retained 4 of 10 and 4 of 12 renal associations, respectively, indicating mixed profile. At Discovery, R398 (kidney atrophy) retained its sole renal association with hypertensive chronic kidney disease after adjustment. sections.title: 2.4 Glyph finds novel associations beyond the clinical literature
sections.content: Having established that Glyph concepts identify significant, reproducible markers of disease risk, we next asked whether they represent novel discoveries beyond those reported in the clinical literature. Specifically, we evaluated 21 future outcomes spanning multiple disease groups. To characterize published abdominal imaging and laboratory markers for these outcomes, an agent acting as co-scientist systematically identified and filtered 342,647 unique publications using the PubMed API54 and Paperclip55 (see Methods for additional details). This yielded 412 literature-derived markers that could be tested in our data, averaging 19.6 per axis, which we then systematically re-evaluated. These included both singular measurements, such as low albumin, and composite clinical predictors such as FIB-456, which combines age, transaminases and platelet count. Finally, to assess whether Glyph concepts add prognostic value beyond these markers, we selected the top ten Glyph concepts per outcome using evidence from the Discovery Site, excluding excluding concepts that primarily reflect care intensity such as R399 (pacemaker). We then fit one model using the literature-derived markers alone and another combining them with the selected Glyph concepts to test whether Glyph concepts identified prognostic information beyond published markers. Results of percentage gains in AUC are presented in Figure 5b. Both the literature baseline and Glyph enhanced model were fit at the Discovery Site, and evaluated on the pooled Internal Test and External Site #1 cohorts. We found that, per-outcome, literature baselines achieved 0.749 AUC (95% CI 0.7370.761) on held-out data, and that ten Glyph concepts significantly improved this to 0.774 (95% CI 0.7620.785, = 2.66 1028). Observed benefits were most concentrated in metabolic, haematologic and infectious outcomes, averaging relative AUROC improvement of 6.64% (95% CI 5.268.01%). These groups also had 5.0 fewer papers on average (10.9 vs 15.9) than the other groups evaluated, indicating they may be under-researched. We then explored which concepts were driving gains over literature markers. The top ten Glyph concepts per outcome, selected at the Discovery Site, reproduced more frequently in the pooled held-out cohort (64.8%) than the literature-derived marker set (28.2%, = 1.861018), the top ten performing literature markers (41.2%, = 2.54 106), and corresponding Phecodes (54.8%, = 0.062). After adjustment for age, sex and race, reproduction required < 0.05 and the same effect direction as at the Discovery Site. Median confounder-adjusted odds ratios in the pooled evaluation cohort were also significantly higher for Glyph (1.31) than for the literature-derived marker set (1.10, = 5.0 105), the top ten literature markers (1.16, = 5.0 105), and corresponding Phecodes (1.19, = 5.0 105; Figure 5c). direct comparison between Glyph concepts and all Phecodes is provided in Supplementary Section A.2 and Figure 13. Overall, this suggests that Glyph captures prognostic information in abdominal CT cohorts, accessible through FM embeddings, that is either underrepresented in the established clinical literature, or is diﬀicult to measure with conventional clinical markers. To review specific axes in detail, we plotted markers according to their publication dates and assessed which of the ten Glyph concepts were represented among the literature-derived markers. Adding Glyph concepts did not significantly improve AUROC across every axis. For example, no significant improvement was observed for dementia (0.871 to 0.870, = 0.80) or Alzheimers disease (0.840 to 0.842, = 0.71), suggesting little to no additional prognostic information beyond the literature-derived markers for these outcomes. In contrast, for heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF; Figure 5d), Glyph identified risk markers not represented among the literature-derived markers, including I65 (splenomegaly), L84 (azotemia), L127 (cytopenia), L108 (cholestasis), and I87 (uncharacterized hepatobiliary pattern). Adding Glyph concepts significantly improved AUROC by 3.6% from 0.824 to 0.854 (p = 4.7 107). Similarly, along the abdominal health to sepsis axis, adding Glyph concepts significantly increased AUROC by 4.9% from 0.673 to 0.706 (p = 3.2 107; Figure 5e). These gains demonstrate additional prognostic information beyond the evaluated literature-derived markers, including contributions from imaging findings not routinely documented in reports, such as I76.

sections.title: 2.5 Glyph MCP provides an interface for open-ended investigation
sections.content: Finally, we demonstrate how Glyph concepts support open-ended, agentic discovery via the Glyph MCP, through set of illustrative workflows for agents and clinicians. The MCP enables more complex, 14/36 Figure 6. The MCP enables more complex analyses that build on foundational layer of Glyph concepts. In this example, concepts were combined into nodes that competed against one as independent predictors for inclusion in disease model of septicemia. I76 (an undocumented imaging concept linked to septicemia) provided predictive contribution independent of hepatic disease markers, fluid accumulation, BMI, inflammatory markers, malignancy, and evidence of clinical intervention, and contributed to prognostic AUC predictive across three cohorts. user-guided discovery workflows. Targeted disease modeling: Beyond automatic discovery, Glyph concepts can be manually assembled into composite features to test user-defined hypothesis about 15/36 disease, for example testing whether an undocumented imaging concept repeatedly linked to septicemia is confounded by body composition or existing disease markers (Figure 6). Concept ranking for target outcome: user can query the concept space directly in natural language, for example asking for the top associations for future myocardial infarction; the Glyph MCP resolves this to the underlying outcome and returns the concepts with the largest prognostic association among those surviving Bonferroni correction, predominantly drawn from laboratory panels in this example (Extended Figure 8). Outside of discovery, Glyph also brings explainability to typical use of foundation models: Individualized risk explanation: Beyond population-level associations, Glyph concepts can explain an individual patients risk prediction, attributing it to the specific concepts driving that prediction and contextualizing them against population-level evidence (Extended Figure 9). Patients-like-me: Given query patient, Glyph retrieves the most similar patient in the cohort and explains their similarity in terms of shared concepts and the rarity of their joint activation, illustrating how the concept space supports case-based reasoning beyond simple embedding distance (Extended Figure 10).

sections.title: 3 Discussion
sections.content: In this paper we introduced Glyph, method for transforming foundation model (FM) embeddings into engines of scientific discovery. At its core, Glyph supposes that FM embeddings, trained on large volumes of clinical data, encode established clinical markers alongside unexplored features that could reveal new insights into disease mechanisms. To extract these features, Glyph builds on mechanistic interpretability and establishes their value as coded, interpretable clinical concepts for scientific investigation. In our dataset, the resulting set of extracted concepts enabled rediscovery of established organ-specific and systemic risk markers associated with the onset of future disease. In addition, we were able to automatically establish that many of these findings were reproducible across three sites without model retraining. Transforming embeddings into separate, interpretable and measurable concepts enabled adjustment for potential confounders identified directly from the data, beyond routinely collected covariates or those selected from prior clinical knowledge. Applying Glyph on large clinical datasets revealed complementary associations and risk factors not reported in established clinical literature. Moreover, complementing literature-derived markers with Glyph concepts significantly improved prognostic prediction across several disease axes. Together, these findings demonstrate that interpretability can extend beyond mechanistic understanding of neural networks, enabling features learned implicitly by FMs to interact directly with existing clinical knowledge and available clinical outcomes. Glyph rediscovered known patterns of disease progression across hepatic, renal, and cardiovascular axes. It also recovered known cross-system associations, e.g. linking renal decline to metabolic comorbidities or valvular atherosclerosis to cardiovascular and neurological disease. Our observations also reflected the complementary strengths of different clinical modalities. Specifically, laboratory concepts more consistently captured renal disease progression than kidney-related imaging findings. Similarly, imagingderived findings often showed more reproducible associations than findings documented in radiology reports, particularly for atherosclerotic and hepatic risk markers. Confounder adjustment further characterized discovered associations by attenuating associations known to involve nonspecific markers of illness severity, such as fluid accumulation and hypoalbuminemia. It also emphasized published prognostic relationships, including associations of imaging-derived vascular findings with neurological outcomes37, renal findings with downstream cardiovascular outcomes57, and the renal consequences of cholestatic liver disease58. Together, the recovery of known disease relationships in patients undergoing abdominal CT supported the validity of the concept space as foundation for the exploration of novel hypotheses. Beyond rediscoveries, Glyph expanded the clinical picture of disease risk, revealing prognostic information beyond what established literature-derived markers capture. In particular, comparisons across modalities highlighted laboratory markers such as cholestasis and cytopenia. After adjustment, these markers retained broad systemic risk profiles, while other laboratory concepts showed more specific associations. Azotemia, for example, retained predominantly renal, metabolic, and hematological risk profile. Beyond laboratory markers, Glyph uncovered previously uncharacterized imaging phenotypes within CT embeddings, including mixed hepatobiliary pattern whose adjusted associations remained significant across all outcome groups. Furthermore, complementing literature-derived markers with selection of top performing Glyph concepts reproducibly improved prognostic prediction, particularly in 16/36 metabolic, hematological and infectious outcomes, indicating that existing published markers lack prognostic information presently available in abdominal CT and laboratory data. Together, these findings demonstrate practical approach to exploring systems-level perspective on disease59, 60 using routinely acquired clinical data. They also motivate evaluating several laboratory markers and imaging phenotypes as potential targets for opportunistic or incidental screening. Comparison with coded phenotypes further characterized the clinical information captured by Glyph. Phecodes, which group ICD codes into clinically meaningful categories, provide an established basis for automated PheWAS discovery2. In some cases, directly matched Phecodes showed the same disease associations as Glyph concepts, but with overall smaller effects that often did not reach significance. For these clinical findings, the stronger signal captured by Glyph enabled both rediscoveries and candidate discoveries that were not detected using diagnosis codes alone. Where Phecodes yielded stronger associations, they reflected related conditions captured in the broader clinical record, beyond the scope of abdominal CT and laboratory data. Across the selected outcomes, this broader coverage yielded more significant associations overall, whereas Glyph associations had larger median effects and higher reproduction rates. Together, these findings suggest that Glyph complements the coded record by making additional phenotypic information in imaging and laboratory data accessible for discovery. Several clinical and technical considerations are important in interpreting our findings. Primarily, our selection criteria restricted the cohorts to patients undergoing abdominal CT across acute and outpatient settings. This selection likely enriched the study population for abdominal illness, influencing both the associations detected and their estimated prognostic value. For example, enrichment for abdominal disease in this cohort may have contributed to the prominence of markers of hepatobiliary disease and renal dysfunction, such as cholestasis and azotemia. In addition, enrichment for abdominal disease could partly explain why hepatobiliary abnormalities featured among the strongest adjusted markers of cardiovascular outcomes, alongside established vascular, renal and haematological risk markers. Future work could reproduce these analyses in broader patient populations to assess whether the observed associations and relative prognostic value of these markers are preserved. Furthermore, outcome data used in our study warrant further consideration. We used Phecodes derived from ICD codes as outcome data to standardize evaluation across institutions2. However, such coded data may introduce noise and uncertainty, e.g. regarding the precise timing of observed disease patterns. Consequently, some associations may capture existing but undocumented disease rather than risk of future disease onset, while cases never assigned the corresponding code may be missed entirely. Refining outcome labels through clinician adjudication of longitudinal records against predefined diagnostic criteria could correct diagnosis and timing, but would require extensive chart review, potentially supported by automated search of clinical notes. Ultimately, prospective studies using predefined diagnostic criteria and systematic follow-up would be required for stronger validation of these outcomes. Glyph enabled systematic confounder adjustment across broad set of clinical concepts. Associations that persist after adjustment indicate that related concepts provide prognostic information beyond clinical covariates and other identified concepts, but do not establish that they represent independent disease processes or causal drivers of disease on retrospective dataset. Broader clinical coverage, including additional imaging, clinical notes, categorical laboratory results, flowsheets, medication use, and genetic factors, could help account for omitted factors and reveal further confounders and candidate markers. Furthermore, the fixed correlation threshold used in our analysis was designed to exclude potential mediators, downstream consequences through which the tested concept could affect the outcome, but adjustment results were sensitive to the chosen threshold. Future work should guide confounder selection using knowledge of disease mechanisms, rather than statistics alone61. Future work could extend the systematic comparison with published literature presented in Section 2.4 beyond the selected outcomes. Although it requires substantial token usage, this assessment provides framework for distinguishing established relationships recovered by Glyph, published associations not detected in our cohorts, and potentially novel findings. Future work could also investigate how concepts change over time and how their combinations contribute to disease risk. The analyses shown in this work related concepts measured around individual CT examinations to future outcomes. Repeated measurement could reveal when concepts emerge, how they evolve, and how their relationships change through disease progression, providing temporal evidence to guide causal investigation. Combined with more 17/36 complete treatment histories, these trajectories could support investigation of changes associated with clinical intervention. Changes in concept activation could also be evaluated as quantitative indicators of disease state or treatment response by comparing their sensitivity with existing clinical measures. Beyond these temporal extensions, our PheWAS analysis tested concepts individually and did not assess their combined prognostic information. Future work could examine combinations and interactions between concepts to identify more specific clinical phenotypes and risk associations not apparent from individual markers. Technical considerations and insights arise both from the source embeddings and from how their features are extracted and interpreted. Text embeddings yielded finer-grained concepts than image embeddings, even though radiology reports provide compressed description of the images. This observation motivates future work in designing image encoders for fine-grained concept discovery, alongside methods for resolving more specific findings within existing embeddings. We also extracted embeddings separately by modality, which simplified attribution of concepts to their source and examination of relationships across modalities. However, some predictive patterns may be inherently multimodal, motivating joint embeddings that could capture combinations of imaging, laboratory, and report findings not fully represented in any single modality. One insight from our confounder analyses is that prediction models built on FM embeddings can draw on both potentially actionable markers and confounded proxies for illness. Risk scores derived from the full FM embedding may therefore identify patients at risk without reliably guiding how that risk can be reduced. Textual interpretations describe the clinical findings associated with feature, but do not necessarily establish its precise clinical meaning. In subset of extracted concepts, automated interpretation required combination of small number of distinct clinical or imaging findings, suggesting that not all concepts were monosemantic. It remains unclear whether this reflects polysemanticity in the FM embeddings, failure of the SAE to separate distinct features, or property of underlying data, in which certain features frequently co-occur making feature separation diﬀicult. Clinical knowledge could guide when related concepts should be grouped or separated into more specific findings, with Glyph providing an eﬀicient basis for refining and testing these definitions. Future work could also complement our global evaluation with local comparisons against neighboring concepts and clinically similar cases that do not activate the concept in question. These comparisons could help distinguish defining findings from cooccurring data properties, severity, or clinical context. In conclusion, Glyph provides framework for extracting knowledge from foundation models, enabling reproducible, population-scale discovery of disease markers and associations. Glyph can be applied to any dataset represented by FM embeddings to rapidly investigate chosen discovery axis, using an agentic co-scientist framework to assess the novelty and added value of extracted findings against the published literature. This enables researchers to automatically validate data-driven insights, such as those presented here, or discover and share new concept networks and insights from their own datasets. Overall, we envision that Glyph can accelerate clinical science by establishing standard for sharing validated FM features as data-driven phenotypes, connecting discoveries across datasets with existing clinical knowledge. 18/

sections.title: 4.1 Datasets
sections.content: All datasets are partitioned into Discovery Site and series of Testing sets. The Discovery Site is used to train sparse autoencoders, select disease outcomes, interpret concepts, and rank associations. Testing sets are held out entirely and used solely to assess whether insights replicate in patient cohorts that played no part in discovery, in order of increasing institutional distance from Stanford. All datasets were collected under IRB approval with waiver of informed consent owing to retrospective use. Discovery Site Stanford Main hospital. The Discovery Site cohort comprises consecutive abdominal CT examinations performed at Stanford academic medical center from December 2012 to October 2018, yielding 20,391 CT studies from 14,652 unique patients (3,262,560 CT slices, 1,588,003 lab entries, and 22,781,540 historical diagnoses). No patient contributed studies to more than one split. We divide the cohort into train set of 15,331 studies from 11,009 patients (2,452,960 slices, 6,083,609 report tokens, 1,194,451 lab entries, 17,017,170 diagnoses) and validation set of 5,060 studies from 3,643 patients (809,600 slices, 2,000,273 report tokens, 393,552 lab entries, 5,764,373 diagnoses). Embedding normalization statistics are computed on the Discovery Site. Finally, all datasets contain abdominal CT images and radiology reports that capture the current health of the patient; laboratory analyses are restricted to the Discovery Site, Internal Test and External Site #1. All have longitudinal ICD codes with at least 4 years of follow-up for association studies, and the six universal clinical covariates, including race. CT preprocessing follows14. From each study, the series with the greatest number of axial slices was selected to maximize information content, and contrast-phase detection algorithm confirmed that 97% of selected series were portal venous phase. Volumes were preprocessed by orienting axes (leftright, posterioranterior, inferiorsuperior), resampling to 1.5 mm in-plane resolution and 3 mm slice thickness, clipping and normalizing Hounsfield units from [1000, 1000] to [0, 1], and center-cropping to 224 224 160 voxels. Report preprocessing follows14. Only the findings section of each report was used, as it provides the most granular per-organ-system observations. It covers the lower thorax, liver and biliary tree, gallbladder, spleen, pancreas, adrenal glands, kidneys and ureters, gastrointestinal tract, peritoneal cavity, pelvic organs, vasculature and lymph nodes, and musculoskeletal system. Longitudinal lab measurements were collected from the EHR for each patient. Only numerical lab types were retained, defined as those where at least 90% of recorded measurements were numeric, resulting in 350 lab types (Supplementary Table 10). To reduce noise in dense measurement periods, quarterly downsampling strategy was applied, retaining only the last recorded value per patient, lab type, and calendar quarter, using only measurements taken within the year prior to the CT scan date. Each lab value was z-score normalized per lab type and clamped to [3, 3] to limit the influence of extreme outliers. For each patient encounter associated with CT scan, all ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes assigned during that encounter were collected and mapped to hierarchical phenotypes using PheWAS Phecode mapping2, collapsing 16,553 distinct ICD codes to 1,692 phenotype categories. Internal Test cohort Stanford Main hospital. The Internal Test cohort contains 5,137 CT studies from 3,667 unique patients drawn from the same institution as the Discovery Site (821,920 CT slices, 405,802 lab entries, 6,134,090 diagnoses). These patients were held out from all stages of discovery and represent the first test of reproducibility under matched distributional conditions. External Site #1. The External Site #1 cohort contains 25,803 CT studies from 17,224 patients at community hospital outside Stanford (4,128,480 CT slices, 1,764,079 lab entries, 19,610,547 diagnoses). No data from this cohort was used at any stage of discovery or model training, and the shift in patient population and clinical practice makes it more demanding test of generalization. External Site #2 Mayo Clinic. The Mayo Clinic cohort consists of patients across four Mayo Clinic hospitals, comprising 14,199 CT studies from 6,085 patients. No data from this cohort was used 22/36 at any stage of discovery or model training, and as an out-of-state health system it represents the greatest institutional distance from the Discovery Site. sections.title: 4.2 Foundation Models
sections.content: Each data modality is encoded by the most performant foundation model chosen at the time of the study. FM weights are frozen throughout all downstream analyses; the SAEs and association pipelines operate entirely on static embeddings produced by these models. CT imaging For CT images, we use Merlin14, 3D inflated ResNet-152 pretrained on abdominal CT volumes paired with radiology reports and EHR diagnosis codes. Merlin processes each CT volume and produces 2,048-dimensional embedding that serves as the input to all downstream concept extraction and association analyses. CT radiology report For radiology report findings, we use Qwen3-Embedding-8B21, general-domain text embedding model selected as the top-performing model on the MTEB leaderboard at the time of this study62. Each findings section is encoded into single 4,096-dimensional vector. Laboratory values We use EHR Labs FM, an in-house masked autoencoder pretrained on laboratory histories from the Discovery Site. The encoder is three-layer Feature Tokenizer Transformer with four attention heads and hidden dimension of 768 that jointly encodes laboratory values, test types and measurement times. For each history, values are randomly masked at rate sampled uniformly between 0 and 90%, with at least one value masked. Laboratory-specific prediction heads reconstruct the masked values using mean squared error objective. Training uses AdamW with learning rate of 104, batch size of 256 and 1,500 optimisation steps, with checkpoint selection based on validation reconstruction loss. For downstream analyses, the reconstruction heads are discarded and the encoder remains frozen. Its output embeddings are averaged over non-padding tokens to produce single 768-dimensional vector.

sections.title: 4.3 Sparse Autoencoders
sections.content: FM embeddings are dense and polysemantic: individual dimensions typically encode mixtures of unrelated clinical concepts simultaneously, making direct interpretation infeasible. Sparse autoencoders address this by learning larger, overcomplete dictionary of directions in the embedding space, where each sample activates only small subset of dictionary entries. This sparsity encourages each entry to correspond to single, distinct clinical concept. 23/36 Architecture. For each modality, separate SAE operates on the z-normalized FM embedding = (x µ)/σ, where statistics are computed on the Discovery train set. Z-normalization is critical so that the SAE learns relative structure in the embedding space rather than the distance of all points from the origin. linear encoder maps to pre-activation scores over dictionary of = 8,192 features, = xWenc + benc, Wenc Rdn (1) and Top-K sparsity retains only the highest-scoring features, zeroing the rest to produce the sparse representation zsparse = TopK(z, K). linear decoder then reconstructs the embedding, ˆx = zsparseWdec + bdec, Wdec Rnd. (2) The decoder is initialized as the transpose of the encoder, and its columns are constrained to unit norm throughout training, with the gradient component parallel to each column removed after each step to prevent shrinkage. We ablate five sparsity levels, {5, 10, 20, 40, 80}. Matryoshka SAEs. Standard Top-K SAEs tend to produce only fine-grained features, phenomenon known as feature splitting, neglecting broader concepts higher in the clinical hierarchy. To address this, we additionally train Matryoshka SAEs63, which impose nested reconstruction losses across an ordered set of prefix sizes , LMatryoshka = 1 mM zsparse[:m]Wdec[:m, :] bdec2 2 . (3) Smaller prefixes are forced to encode coarser concepts while larger prefixes introduce progressively finer distinctions, producing hierarchical concept space. We test standard Top-K SAE and two Matryoshka SAE configurations, with nested dictionary sizes M1 = {128, 512, 2048, 8192} and M2 = {256, 1024, 4096, 16384}. Training. SAEs are trained on the Discovery train set by minimizing MSE reconstruction loss, = 2, using the Adam optimizer with learning rate of 5 104, batch size of 2,000, and maximum ˆx2 of 1,000 steps with early stopping based on validation loss. One SAE is trained per modality. Feature extraction and configuration selection. Once trained, SAE weights are frozen and sparse features are inferred on all datasets by passing each FM embedding through the pretrained SAE. Each sparse feature is then z-normalized by subtracting its mean and dividing by its standard deviation, both computed on the Discovery Site, providing consistent basis for comparison across modalities and datasets. Based on the ablation results described in Supplementary Section A.3 and Figure 14, we select = 40 with the = {128, 512, 2048, 8192} Matryoshka architecture as single consistent configuration across all modalities. The resulting sparse feature vectors from each modality are concatenated to form unified multimodal concept space, in which each sample is represented by single sparse vector spanning imaging, report, and laboratory concepts.

sections.title: 4.4 Automated Interpretability
sections.content: By design, sparse features activate for only small subset of samples. This sparsity creates the precondition for interpretability: if feature fires for restricted, coherent cohort, it may encode single identifiable clinical phenomenon. To convert features into named concepts at scale, we automate the interpretation process using large language model (LLM), eliminating the need for manual inspection of thousands of features. Generative interpretation. For each SAE feature, we identify the samples in the Discovery Site whose activation exceeds the 75th percentile of all positive activations, forming high-activating cohort. We then present nhigh = 20 randomly sampled high-activating samples to an LLM, alongside nnon = 20 randomly sampled samples with zero or near-zero activation as contrast reference. The contrast is essential: it grounds the interpretation in what is specific to the concept rather than what is common across the patient population. The LLM is instructed to reason via explicit chain-of-thought before producing single-sentence summary of the form This cohort is characterized by [interpretation]. We 24/36 use Gemini 2.5 Pro via PHI-safe GCP Vertex instance. Full prompts are provided in Supplementary Section A.4. Discriminative validation. Validation serves two purposes: assessing whether the interpretation faithfully describes the feature, and testing whether this description generalises to held-out sets. For each concept, we sample nhigh = 20 and nnon = 20 from the test set, then crucially we shuffle the combined pool. The LLM receives the textual interpretation together with the shuffled sample data, is informed that exactly half the samples belong to the cohort, and must classify each sample as either belonging to the concept cohort (1) or not (0). Discrimination accuracy, calculated by the fraction of samples correctly classified, is computed on the Internal Test set as measure of monosemanticity, and separately on each external cohort to assess cross-site and -institutional generalization.

sections.title: 4.5 Outcome selection
sections.content: To maximize the potential for rediscoveries and new discoveries, we use an automated approach to select the highest signal outcome targets for exploration using the Discovery Site. We first map 16,553 unique ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes to 1,692 hierarchical phenotypes termed Phecodes2. From these we define candidate pool of 1,278 outcomes with support in our data. Studies were labeled as progressors if the first recorded diagnosis of an outcome occurred 14 years after the study date. Controls were selected as having no recorded diagnosis of that outcome, and at least four years of follow-up. All other studies, including those with recorded diagnosis of the outcome before the CT date, were excluded from that outcomes analysis. Following64, we then compute on the Discovery Site the aggregate rank (by reciprocal rank fusion) of the ability of each modality and model combination to predict each outcome. The 150 highest-ranked outcomes were then manually reviewed, and nine excluded as not interpretable as clinical disease endpoints. These comprised non-specific catch-all Phecodes (for example, other disorders of the liver), abnormal-finding and administrative codes (for example, other abnormal blood chemistry), and device or procedure status codes (for example, ileostomy status). This left the 141 outcomes used in this study, covering conditions across oncological, cardiovascular, metabolic, and acute disease categories. To see the performance of each FM on this set, see Figure 7.

sections.title: 4.6 Association study
sections.content: Taking inspiration from the multi-stage design of genome-wide association studies2, we estimate the association between each Glyph concept and each future disease outcome as per-standard-deviation odds ratio (OR), enabling direct comparison across modalities whose activations operate on different scales. Standardization. Concept activations are z-normalised using per-site mean and standard deviation, so that each OR reflects the multiplicative change in outcome odds per one standard deviation increase in concept activation. OR computation. For each concept-outcome pair, we fit an unadjusted logistic regression model on the Discovery Site, logit(P(Y = 1)) = α+ βc, (4) where is the standardised concept activation. The per-standard-deviation OR is defined as exp(β), and 95% confidence intervals are reported as exp(β 1.96 SE). Statistical significance. We assess significance using the Wald p-value derived from the asymptotic covariance matrix, computed as the Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse of the Fisher information matrix, I(β) = X, (5) where is diagonal matrix with entries pi(1 pi). The z-statistic = β/SE yields two-tailed p-value. Each CT study was analyzed as separate observation to capture the patients clinical state at the time of imaging, with independence assumed across studies. 25/36 Discovery filter. To concentrate downstream analysis on statistically supported, directionally consistent associations, we apply Bonferroni correction across all concept-outcome pairs, setting the threshold at pBonferroni = 0.05/Npairs = 8.28 108. We additionally require OR > 1.0 to restrict attention to predictive rather than protective associations. Associations satisfying both criteria on the Discovery Site form the set of promising associations carried forward into all subsequent analyses.

sections.title: 4.7 Reproducibility filter
sections.content: Having identified significant associations on the Discovery Site, we assess whether they represent real, generalizable phenomena by re-evaluating them on held-out cohorts. Concept activations on held-out data are computed by applying the same frozen SAE weights without modification, requiring no manual labeling or recalibration of new samples. For each promising association, we re-compute the same OR on each held-out cohort and apply the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure at 5% false discovery rate across the set of re-evaluated associations. An association is considered reproducible if the BH-adjusted p-value is significant and directionality is maintained (OR > 1.0). sections.title: 4.8 Confounder adjustment
sections.content: A predictive association between concept and an outcome may be driven by shared confounder rather than by direct relationship. To assess whether associations persist after adjustment for measured confounders, we apply double machine learning (DML) with cross-fitting65. This allows us to account for nonlinear relationships and interactions among measured confounders that logistic regression with linear covariate terms may miss. The estimator uses Neyman-orthogonal estimating equation, whose expectation is locally insensitive to first-order errors in the nuisance functions at their true values. Orthogonality therefore reduces sensitivity to nuisance estimation errors, while cross-fitting limits overfitting bias. Because our outcomes are binary, we use logistic partially linear model, logit P(Y = 1 T,W ) = θT + r(W ), (6) for concept activation , binary outcome , and confounder set , where θ is the adjusted log-odds ratio of interest and r(W ) is the baseline log-odds function. We estimate the nuisance functions using XGBoost with five-fold outer and five-fold inner cross-fitting, so that each observation is evaluated using nuisance models fitted without that observation. All nuisance construction, including inner cross-fitting, is confined to the corresponding outer training fold. Models use 100 trees with maximum depth four. Each CT study is treated as an independent observation, and activations and continuous covariates are standardized using Discovery training statistics. Baseline log-odds (r). We estimate r(W ) using the Full Model Refitting procedure of Liu et al.66. Within each outer training fold, joint model of on (T,W ) produces inner out-of-fold predictions of the full conditional probability. Their logits serve as an intermediate target for estimating preliminary exposure coeﬀicient and the baseline function r(W ), accounting for the concepts contribution to the full predictor. 26/36 Residualized activation ( ). For the sigmoid-based score used here, orthogonality requires varianceweighted conditional mean of the concept activation67, m(W ) = E[v(T,W )T ] E[v(T,W ) ] , v(T,W ) = µ(T,W ){1 µ(T,W )}, (7) where µ(T,W ) = P(Y = 1 T,W ). We estimate m(W ) by regressing on , with variance weights calculated from the inner out-of-fold predictions of the full outcome model. The fitted weighted regressor is applied to the outer held-out fold to obtain residuals Ti = Ti ˆm(Wi). The adjusted effect ˆθ is then obtained by solving the orthogonal score equation (Yi σ(θTi + ˆr(Wi))) Ti = 0, (8) by root-finding, where σ is the logistic sigmoid function. Standard errors are calculated using the corresponding sandwich estimator. We report the adjusted OR as exp( ˆθ), with 95% Wald confidence interval and two-sided Wald p-value testing θ = 0. Confounder selection. For each association, confounders are drawn from two sources. The six universal clinical covariates are patient age, sex, BMI, alcohol use, smoking status and race, with race represented by indicator variables. In addition, up to ten conceptual confounders are automatically selected per outcome from the significant Glyph associations ranked by unadjusted OR. These are selected independently within each dataset to account for differences between institutions and populations. This also provides the opportunity to test confounders from other modalities, though we disallow confounders from the radiology report to interfere with those from the image, and vice versa, as they were derived from the same data source. To limit overadjustment for overlapping representations of the tested concept and potential mediators, we applied correlation threshold. We selected an absolute Pearson correlation threshold of 0.35 through qualitative inspection to balance excluding likely downstream consequences against retaining potential confounders, and excluded candidates at or above this threshold. For example, when testing ascites, broader concept combining ascites, anasarca, and pleural effusion was excluded from the adjustment set (r=0.61). Similarly, when testing aortic atherosclerosis, broader concept representing abdominopelvic atherosclerosis was excluded (r=0.41). However, related atherosclerosis and aortic calcification concepts remained eligible for adjustment when analyzing aortic atherosclerosis (r=0.310.34), whereas upstream liver pathology was excluded when analyzing splenomegaly (r=0.46). The threshold therefore served as heuristic, since correlation alone cannot distinguish overlapping representations, mediators, and confounders61. Confounder filter. Similar to the Reproducibility filter, an association is considered to survive confounder adjustment if the BH-adjusted p-value (at 5% FDR, applied to the full set of Bonferronisignificant associations) remains significant and the adjusted OR > 1.0. Adjustment was evaluated for the 4,463 significant Discovery associations in each cohort, except at External Site #2, where only the 3,109 imaging and radiology report associations were evaluated.
