Unlike the association filters  (Table 2)  , every cohort, including Discovery, uses BenjaminiHochberg threshold (5% FDR) computed over the confounder-adjusted p-values of the promising associations tested on that cohort. Inter-concept causal graph. To recover directed relationships among concepts, we learned single sparse directed acyclic graph (DAG) over all documented and undocumented concepts together with fixed set of universal confounders (age, sex, smoking status, heavy alcohol use, and BMI) as additional nodes, allowing the structure learner to attribute shared demographic and lifestyle variation to edges from the confounder nodes rather than to spurious concept-concept edges (see Figure 11). We standardized all 27/36 node activations and fit linear structural equation model = XW + ε with an ℓ1 sparsity penalty on the weighted adjacency , subject to continuous acyclicity constraint. We used DAGMA68, which enforces acyclicity through log-determinant characterization and continuation schedule that progressively tightens the constraint toward an exact DAG, building on the continuous-optimization formulation of NOTEARS69. Entries of below magnitude threshold were set to zero, and the surviving weights define the directed edges. Whereas the primary concept-outcome analyses use double machine learning (DML), which is confounder-robust but requires fitting separate nuisance models per target65, the interconcept graph involves on the order of d2 candidate relationships across all concepts, making per-pair DML computationally prohibitive; we therefore learn the full structure, confounders included, in single continuous optimization and reserve DML for the smaller, hypothesis-driven outcome analyses in the main text. This procedure is an approximate analog to confounder adjustment rather than guarantee of it: concept-concept edge is adjusted for confounder only if that confounders weight survives thresholding, and edge directions reflect the acyclicity constraint and model fit rather than verified causal mechanisms. Unexpected edges may thus reflect genuine population-specific structure, but could also stem from residual confounding or artifacts of thresholding and optimization.

sections.title: 4.9 Comparison with the clinical literature
sections.content: To assess whether Glyph identifies prognostic information beyond established clinical markers, we compared its concepts with risk markers reported in the literature. Here, we describe the literature search and screening, reconstruction of published markers, and methods used to compare their associations and predictive value with Glyph. For each outcome, PubMed and Paperclip queries combined endpoint names and synonyms with an input scope defining eligible abdominal imaging findings, laboratory measurements and clinical risk factors. Publication in leading relevant journal or at least 50 citations was required, retaining 83,649 outcome-specific records. Title screening advanced 14,801 records to abstract review, of which 4,748 underwent further assessment of their measurements, endpoints and local feasibility. Original methods and tables were consulted where marker definitions were unclear. At least one reported marker could be reconstructed for 1,822 records, before deduplicating repeated measurement families and selecting 293 representative studies. later report-based COPD marker was included outside the initial impact criterion, bringing the total to 294. Markers were reconstructed using published thresholds, transformations and compositescore definitions, with approximate measurements labelled as proxies. Counting markers separately for each outcome, the final 412 entries comprised 36 explicit multi-input scores, ratios or biomarker rules (8.7%), 31 BMI or estimated kidney-function measures (7.5%), and 345 single measurements, findings or recorded conditions (83.7%). Thus, 67 markers (16.3%) combined multiple inputs under the broader definition including BMI and estimated kidney function. Queries, source papers, screening decisions and fitted definitions were retained for each outcome. All prediction models used the same outcome-eligible CT studies and included age, sex and recorded race. Markers required at least 100 observed Discovery measurements and, for binary rules, at least 25 observations in each category. Missing measurements were replaced with the Discovery training mean and accompanied by missingness indicator. Ridge logistic regression coeﬀicients and preprocessing were learned on Discovery training data, with regularization selected by validation AUROC and the selected model applied without refitting. Models were fitted to convergence before validation AUROC was used to select regularization. Patients did not cross fitting, tuning or evaluation splits. We repeated fitting on five bootstrap samples of independent Discovery training studies, keeping the concept sets, validation set and held-out cohorts fixed. Reported AUROCs are the arithmetic means of the five fittedmodel AUROCs, rather than AUROCs of averaged predictions. If an augmented model did not improve validation AUROC, the corresponding baseline was retained. Evaluation used the pooled Internal Test and External Site #1 cohorts. External Site #2 was not included because direct access to the clinical data needed to reconstruct the literature markers was unavailable at the time of the study. AUROC confidence intervals and two-sided comparisons used paired study-level influence functions averaged across the five fits. Across-outcome means gave outcomes equal weight, retaining shared-study covariance across models and outcomes; relative-gain uncertainty used the delta method. Inference conditions on the fitted models and selected markers and does not include training or selection uncertainty. 28/36 Individual-marker associations were estimated using the orthogonal logistic DML estimator described above, adjusted for age, sex and recorded race, with five-fold outer and inner cross-fitting and independentstudy sandwich uncertainty. Exposures, including binary rules, were standardized using Discovery training statistics. Ten Glyph concepts per outcome were curated using Discovery clinically adjusted rankings and clinical interpretations, excluding concepts primarily reflecting intervention or workflow. For the size-matched OR and reproduction comparisons, up to ten literature markers per outcome were selected using the adjusted Discovery-site OR ranking and fixed across held-out cohorts. This selection did not restrict the literature baseline used in the prediction models. There were 194 selected literature markers across outcomes. Reproduction required BH-adjusted < 0.05 in the pooled held-out cohort and the same effect direction as Discovery, with BH applied across the 768 Glyph, literature and matched-Phecode markeroutcome associations. Differences in reproduction rates were tested using two-sided Fisher exact tests, treating reproduction of each association as independent. Median OR comparisons gave outcomes equal weight and used 20,000 shared-study multiplier bootstrap samples to preserve dependence across markers and outcomes, with marker sets and nuisance fits fixed. The minimum attainable bootstrap p-value was 1/20,001. BenjaminiHochberg correction was applied to the six displayed held-out OR comparisons, with separate families for the three Discovery and three pooled comparisons. KDEs used all supported outcomes within each marker family; pairwise median comparisons used the outcomes supported by both families.

To make analysis more token-eﬀicient, we only interpret high-risk concepts, defined by those with at least one significant association to future disease (see Section 2.2). Prior work highlighted the diﬀiculty of interpreting radiological SAE features at an F1 threshold of 0.7570, motivating our choice of discrimination accuracy threshold of 75% for considering concept interpretable. Using this method and threshold, 88.6% of radiology report concepts were interpretable internally, and 76.6% and 86.7% of interpretations successfully generalized to External Sites #1 and #2, respectively (see Figure 12c). This high rate was expected, as these concepts are derived from embeddings of text that explicitly describe clinical findings. Interpreting concepts derived from images represents greater challenge, as Merlin likely relies on its own internal set of concepts that may not correspond to anything radiologists routinely or consistently document in reports. Remarkably, 52.5% of Merlin image concepts were broadly interpretable by corresponding radiology reports (see Figure 12df). Labs concepts were more automatically interpretable than imaging (see Figure 12gi), and captured physiological states such as monocytosis. Investigating image concepts not interpretable by AutoInterp, we find many still carry identifiable meaning, when viewed directly in images by radiologists. For example, we noticed I76 was not interpretable via AutoInterp, but was among the top 1% closest imaging-derived markers to broad swath of laboratory concepts, spanning inflammation, cholesterol, and protein levels (annotated in 2b). Strikingly, despite not being routinely documented, I76 was significantly associated with the onset of infection, sepsis, septicemia, and wasting. Prompted by these results, radiologists visually inspected images retrieved by this concept, finding it activates in patients with severely distended, fluid-filled bowel loops (see Figure 12de). A.2 Glyph provided complementary associations to pre-coded phenotypes Having established that Glyph concepts yield significant and reproducible markers of future disease risk, we asked whether pre-coded PheWAS for automated clinical discovery would have identified the same discoveries2. We treated Phecodes as exposures and applied the same discovery pipeline, including multiple-test corrected Discovery and Reproducibility filters, searching among the same 141 outcomes where Glyph has the maximum expected yield. Aggregate binary-exposure results are presented in Figure 13ab. Recent Phecodes recorded from 180 to +30 days relative to the scan yielded 7,843 promising associations, with significantly lower replication than Glyph concepts at Internal Test (47.2% vs. 69.3%, = 9.77 104) and External Site #1 (59.9% vs. 74.3%, = 1.95 103) Using each patients entire recorded coding history increased the Phecode yield to 15,274 promising associations, approximately 3.4 the number identified by Glyph, of which 49.1% and 63.9% reproduced in the two held-out cohorts. The median Discovery-site effect was smaller for both Phecode arms than for Glyph concepts (OR 1.29 for Recent Phecodes and 1.33 for all-history Phecodes, versus 1.45 for Glyph). The greater yield reflects the broader scope of ICD codes, which span the full medical record, whereas Glyph concepts were limited to phenomena observable in abdominal CT images, and laboratory panels. Comparable yield may therefore be possible as Glyph expands to additional modalities and examinations. We next assessed which Glyph associations could have been identified from codes alone (see Figure 13c). For previously reported associations, we identified if there was matching Phecode and compared their associations directly. Directly matched associations were often recoverable from Phecodes. For example, Phecode 571.51 (cirrhosis of the liver) reproducibly predicted primary liver cancer (OR 2.03 2.25), independently corroborating the association identified for R85 (cirrhotic liver morphology and varices; OR 1.642.55). Across the majority of comparisons with matching Phecode, the Glyph concept had larger odds ratio. Some matched Phecodes did not pass the Discovery filter, and some additional Glyph associations had no corresponding Phecode. Overall, Phecodes identified more associations across the full medical record, while Glyph concepts yielded larger median effects, reproduced more frequently, 2/36 Figure 12. Glyph concepts are automatically extracted, interpreted, and reproduced zero-shot at external sites. Each concept is interpreted on the Discovery Site by comparing topversus non-activating examples, then re-extracted at an Internal Test cohort and two external sites where the same interpretation is re-tested on unseen patients; consistent discrimination shows both concepts and interpretations transfer across institutions. ac radiology report concept, labeled metastatic disease, re-extracted zero-shot and confirmed at every site. AutoInterp accuracy is highest for reports: as human-written summaries, their concepts are near-fully interpretable but bounded in discovery potential. de An imaging concept whose interpretation is not consistently documented in radiology reports, yet was found to rank among the top 10% of imaging predictors of infection, sepsis, wasting, and organ failure. Remarkably, 52.5% of imaging concepts were interpretable via corresponding radiology reports. gi laboratory concept, labelled monocytosis or neutrophilia, confirmed across sites. 3/36 Figure 13. Glyph concepts build on pre-coded discovery. Phecodes group ICD codes into manually curated, clinically meaningful concepts for use in research2. We test complementary benefits of data-driven Glyph concepts over Phecodes. ab Binary Phecodes drawn from the full recorded history yield 3.4 more significant associations than Glyph concepts, but reproduce less often at Internal Test (49% versus 69%) and have smaller median effect (OR 1.33 versus 1.45). Recent Phecodes, restricted to the scan-adjacent window, also yield more associations than Glyph concepts but reproduce less often. Directly corresponding Phecodes were often less specific than imagingor laboratory-derived Glyph concepts and yielded weaker or nonsignificant associations. In other cases, the broader clinical history captured by Phecodes provided stronger proxy for future risk. For example, hypertension served as proxy for atherosclerosis (bottom) and outperformed the corresponding Glyph concept for some outcomes. and produced stronger associations within directly matched phenotypes. Phecodes therefore capture information beyond the modalities available to Glyph, while Glyph concepts extract more predictive signal from the modalities it does observe. 4/ A.3 Architectural ablations The quality of Glyphs concept space, and hence the sensitivity of all downstream discovery, depended directly on the architecture of the sparse autoencoder. Two parameters governed standard Top-K SAEs: sparsity K, which set the number of features active per sample, and dictionary size N, the maximum number of distinct features available. Standard SAEs, however, have known tendency known as feature splitting to recover only fine-grained concepts while neglecting broader phenomena higher in the conceptual hierarchy. The Matryoshka SAE addressed this by organising features into nested groups of increasing specificity, simultaneously encoding concepts at multiple scales. To identify the architecture best suited to Glyphs multimodal clinical data, we systematically evaluated standard Top-K SAE alongside two Matryoshka variants with nested dictionary sizes [128, 512, 2048, 8192] and [256, 1024, 4096, 16384], across five sparsity levels (K {5, 10, 20, 40, 80}) and all three modalities. Across all modalities, increasing was the dominant factor for improving reconstruction quality, reducing MSE and raising R2 between original and reconstructed FM embeddings (Figure 14ab). All modalities exhibited diminishing returns beyond = 40, beyond which additional active features yielded marginal improvements while increasing computational cost. The number of alive features in the dictionary also grew with K, reflecting the richer encoding capacity afforded by denser activations. Modality differences in the required number of features broadly tracked embedding dimensionality: radiology reports, embedded with the 4096-dimensional Qwen3-Embedding-8B, required more active features than CT images via Merlin (2048-dimensional), which in turn required more than laboratory values via the Labs FM (768-dimensional). Matryoshka SAEs improved generalisation to external data relative to the standard Top-K baseline, an advantage more clearly visible on the External Site #1 cohort than on the internal discovery set. The SAE trained on Discovery data maintained strong performance across all test sets, though with modest drop on external cohorts that mirrored the reduced replication rates in Sections 2.2 and 2.3, and may partly reflect this distributional shift. No meaningful benefit was observed between the two Matryoshka dictionary sizes, and we accordingly selected the Top-K = 40 Matryoshka SAE with nested sizes [128, 512, 2048, 8192] for all analyses, balancing concept quality, generalisation, and computational cost, and achieved over 90% reconstruction of the original embeddings (R2 > 0.90) across all modalities and FMs. Beyond reconstruction fidelity, key requirement was that the sparsified concept space preserved the predictive power of the underlying foundation models, confirming that the interpretability step did not discard clinically relevant signal (Figure 14c). Across modalities, Glyph concepts closely matched FM predictive performance, with particularly tight agreement for CT images (AUC 0.73 vs. 0.73 on the internal test cohort, 0.71 vs. 0.70 on External Site #1) and laboratory values (0.73 vs. 0.71; 0.66 vs. 0.65). Radiology report concepts showed modestly larger gap (0.72 vs. 0.63; 0.68 vs. 0.62), consistent with the greater information density of the high-dimensional Qwen3-Embedding-8B text embedding space. Overall, predictive performance was largely preserved for imaging and laboratory concepts, with larger reductions for radiology report concepts. Lastly, we assessed whether the derived concepts were objectively interpretable to an independent automated judge (Figure 14d). self-reported interpretation could trivially appear coherent, so we instead posed interpretability as discrimination task: second LLM, given only the text interpretation, must classify unseen patients as highor non-activating for that concept. Using the AutoInterp pipeline (see Methods, Section 4.4), interpretations generated on the discovery set were evaluated on unseen patients without modification, testing whether each description accurately characterised new activations of the same concept. Radiology report concepts were highly interpretable, with 88.6% achieving an interpretability score above 75% on the internal test cohort and 76.6% on External Site #1. Laboratory concepts were competitive, with 77.6% achieving above 75% interpretability. CT image concepts were the least interpretable (52.5% on test, 45.5% on External Site #1), plausibly because sparse image features can capture visual structure not routinely documented in paired radiology reports. Overall, we concluded that Glyph produced concept space that is broadly intelligible across all three clinical modalities. 5/36 Figure 14. Results are organized by modality, with panels ac corresponding to CT imaging (Merlin), radiology reports (Qwen3-Embedding-8B), and laboratory values (Labs FM), respectively. These characteristics should be positive, and somewhat unusual to be among so many reporst from different patients at once. Things like 'no evidence of bowel obstruction' is so common it is not useful. The explanation should be general enough to apply to the highest number of reports in this cohort, but not so general that it is no longer specific to this cohort, and would apply to many of the reference patients from the larger dataset. To arrive at the most accurate and precise explanation of what this cohort is characterized by, you must engage in explicit chain of thought reasoning. Pay close attention to recurring terminology, described anatomical structures, and especially consistent pathological findings. Consider how these elements might interrelate to form singular, distinctive feature that the cohort could be characterized by. As you progress through your analysis, verbalize your thought process. Explain each step of your reasoning, from initial observations to intermediate conclusions, and finally to your overall assessment.
